steps.title: التَّوَابِع — words that follow, not lead
body: A تَابِع ("follower") copies some or all of a preceding noun's grammar instead of carrying independent case of its own. Four exist; this lesson covers the first two.

النَّعْت is an adjective that fully agrees with its noun (الْمَنْعُوت) — definiteness, gender, number, AND case, all four: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ جَمِيلٌ ("the big house is beautiful") — الْكَبِيرُ matches الْبَيْتُ on every count. رَأَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ الطَّوِيلَ ("I saw the tall man") shows the same agreement in the accusative.

عَطْف النَّسَق joins two SEPARATE nouns with a conjunction (وَ, أَوْ, and others) and forces the second (الْمَعْطُوف) to take the same case as the first (الْمَعْطُوف عَلَيْه) — even though neither describes the other: الْأَبُ وَالْأُمُّ سَعِيدَانِ ("the father and the mother are happy"); قَرَأْتُ الْكِتَابَ وَالدَّرْسَ ("I read the book and the lesson").

steps.title: Four sentences, two kinds of "following"
steps.intro: Read all four and notice which words are AGREEING (النعت) and which are just SHARING a case (عطف). Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: النَّعْت — full agreement
steps.prompt: الْكَبِيرُ agrees with الْبَيْتُ in four ways. Which of these is NOT one of them?

options.label: Person (1st/2nd/3rd) — nouns don't have this at all

steps.explanation: النَّعْت agrees with its noun in definiteness, gender, number, and case — four things total. "Person" (1st/2nd/3rd) is a property of pronouns and verbs, not nouns or adjectives.

steps.title: النَّعْت follows the case, too
steps.prompt: Why does الطَّوِيلَ end in a fatḥa here, matching الرَّجُلَ?

options.label: الطَّوِيلَ is النَّعْت — it must agree with الرَّجُلَ's accusative case, since الرَّجُلَ is مَفْعُول بِهِ
الطَّوِيلَ is الْحَال — describing a temporary state
All adjectives end in fatḥa by default

steps.explanation: الرَّجُلَ is مَفْعُول بِهِ (accusative). Its نَعْت, الطَّوِيلَ, must copy that case — a mismatched case on the adjective would be an error, not a stylistic choice.

steps.title: عَطْف النَّسَق — sharing a case, not agreeing
steps.prompt: الْأُمُّ takes رَفْع here. Is الْأُمُّ describing الْأَبُ, the way النَّعْت would?

options.label: No — الْأُمُّ is a separate noun conjoined by وَ; it just happens to share الْأَبُ's case
Yes — الْأُمُّ is النَّعْت, describing الْأَبُ
Yes — الْأُمُّ is الْحَال, describing a state

steps.explanation: الْأَبُ and الْأُمُّ are two independent nouns, joined by the conjunction وَ (عَطْف النَّسَق) — neither describes the other. The conjunction just forces the second to copy the first's case, رَفْع, here forming one compound مُبْتَدَأ.

steps.title: عَطْف النَّسَق works on any case

options.label: It's الْمَعْطُوف — conjoined by وَ to الْكِتَابَ, so it copies الْكِتَابَ's accusative case
الدَّرْسَ is always accusative, in any sentence

steps.explanation: عَطْف النَّسَق isn't limited to رَفْع — the conjoined noun copies WHATEVER case the first noun has. Here الْكِتَابَ is نَصْب (مَفْعُول بِهِ), so الدَّرْسَ is نَصْب too.

steps.title: Two followers down, two to go
steps.message: النَّعْت (full agreement, describes its noun) and عَطْف النَّسَق (shares a case, joins two equals) are the first two of the four تَوَابِع. التَّوْكِيد (emphasis) and الْبَدَل (substitution) are still ahead.
